To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the extent of ischemic damage is related to the degree of hypotension and hypoperfusion during progressive ischemia.
the extent of ischemic damage depends on the degree to which local blood flow is reduced and the degree to which the local blood flow is heterogeneously reduced.

the extent of neuronal damage in gerbils subjected to 5-30 min of unilateral carotid ligation is related to the degree of hypotension of local blood flow, and that neuronal vulnerability is not uniform throughout the gerbil brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of cerebral blood flow and neuronal injury in the gerbil model of focal cerebral ischemic injury.
the relationship between local blood flow and ischemic damage in gerbils during progressive cerebral ischemic injury.
the study of the pathogenesis of cerebral ischemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the extent of ischemic damage is related to the duration and degree of local blood flow reduction, but that the extent of local blood flow reductions required to cause irreversible ischemic damage is different in different brain regions.
the more severe the ischemia, the greater the damage.
focal cerebral ischemia is not a homogeneous process and that the severity of ischemic damage depends on local cerebral blood flow and on regional neuronal sensitivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the severity of ischemic neuronal damage in gerbils is determined by the extent of focal ischemia.
the severity of hypoperfusion determines the extent of ischemic damage, and the severity of the hypoperfusion is a major determinant of the degree of ischemic damage.
the severity of ischemic damage is related to the degree of ischemic blood flow, but not to a simple "threshold value."
The main takeaway from our work is that
the degree of hypotension, and not the duration of hypoxia, determines the extent of ischemic damage.
it’s important to look at multiple measures when trying to understand the relationship between ischemic damage and blood flow.
there is no single threshold value for cerebral blood flow below which neuronal damage occurs.
